# Affine sampled support closes a normal sector without incoming correction
transport on actual fiber boundaries. It gives an exact reduced
volume-source law, not a recursive boundary stress or an OC induction.

## 1. Setting and theorem

Let C be a compact convex body in R^n times R^d, d>=1. Let P be all
of its nonempty integer bases, and assume each fiber K_p is a
full-dimensional compact polytope in R^d. Thus P is finite and
lattice-complete in its convex hull. Define the canonical hull

    C_0=conv(union_{p in P} {p} times K_p).

It has exactly the same integer fibers as C. Let eta be the sum of
the intrinsic (d-1)-dimensional own-fiber boundary measures, marked
by the almost-everywhere unique outward unit normal. When d=1 this
is endpoint counting measure, marked by the two signed directions.
Let nu be a finite measure absolutely continuous with respect to eta,
and let Pi be a physical martingale coupling from nu to eta preserving
the continuous normal mark.

Fix a unit vector u. Assume the *sampled* support values in this one
direction are affine in the base:

    h_Kp(u)=a.p+b                       for every p in P.       (1)

Write F_u=C_0 intersect {u.x-a.z=b}. Assume eta(F_u)>0.

**Theorem.** Up to their respective boundary-null sets, the physical
restrictions of eta and nu to F_u are exactly their normal-u sectors.
Consequently

    Pi{w outside F_u, w' in F_u}=0,
    Pi{w in F_u, w' outside F_u}=0,
    nu(F_u)=eta(F_u).                                      (2)

The source rows on F_u therefore couple nu|_F_u to the *entire*
unweighted target eta|_F_u; the incoming correction is zero.

If P affinely spans R^n, C_0 is a full-dimensional compact polytope,
F_u is a nonvertical supporting facet, and its exact affine
straightening gives a full-dimensional compact reduced polytope D in
R^n times R^(d-1). The pulled-back law is

    nu_hat_u <=_cx mu_u,
    mu_u=sum_{p in P} H_(d-1)|_{D_p}.                       (3)

Here zero-measure faces are included with zero weight. The reduced
mixed trace has Hausdorff dimension d-1, so mu_u is also its intrinsic
Hausdorff measure. The law has equal mass and every affine physical
moment. With no assumption on the affine span of P, (2) and the
fiber-measure identity still hold, but no full-dimensional reduced
body in the original n base coordinates is claimed.

Only the single support direction (1) is needed. In particular, if
all support functions of the sampled family are affine in p, this
conclusion holds in every positive boundary-normal sector.

## 2. Canonical support and exact identification of the sector

Because C_0 is contained in C and includes every prescribed fiber,
its section at p is exactly K_p. Its projection is conv(P); an
integer point of that projection belongs to P because C already has
a nonempty fiber there. Thus taking the canonical hull changes
neither the integer base set nor the integer fibers.

Equation (1) implies

    u.x-a.z <= b on C_0,

and its exposed face is exactly the convex hull of the exposed
u-faces of the K_p, placed over their bases. Indeed all generating
points satisfy the supporting inequality, and a convex combination
attains equality only when each positively weighted point does.
At every actual base,

    (F_u)_p = {x in K_p: u.x=h_Kp(u)}.                    (4)

For a full-dimensional polytope K_p, almost every own-boundary point
with outward normal u lies in the face (4). Conversely, if (4) has
dimension d-1, its relative interior has unique outward unit normal
u and its other boundary points have H_(d-1) measure zero. If it has
smaller dimension, it carries zero boundary measure. For d=1 its
nonempty face is exactly the endpoint with the appropriate signed
normal. It follows that, as marked measures,

    eta|_F_u = eta|_{normal=u}.                           (5)

Absolute continuity gives the same equality for nu. A
normal-preserving coupling cannot enter or leave a normal sector.
Using (5) for both marginals proves both zero-crossing statements in
(2), and hence equality of their masses. This proof of zero incoming
mass uses normal preservation, not an unjustified disjointness of
ambient facet owners. The physical martingale condition is then
retained by the restricted rows and supplies (3) after straightening.

If P spans R^n, C_0 has dimension n+d because it contains a
full-dimensional continuous fiber and its projection spans R^n.
The face F_u projects onto all of conv(P), since every exposed fiber
face is nonempty. Positive eta(F_u) supplies at least one vertical
(d-1)-dimensional face within F_u. Its direction space is u-perp.
Together with n independent projected base directions this gives
dimension at least n+d-1. The supporting hyperplane has that exact
dimension, proving that F_u is an ambient facet.

## 3. Reduced body, metric, and source law

Let E:R^(d-1) -> u-perp be a linear isometry, with the usual
zero-dimensional convention for d=1. Put

    Psi(z,t)=(z,Et+(a.z+b)u),
    D=Psi^(-1)(F_u).                                     (6)

This is an affine bijection onto the supporting hyperplane, keeping
the integer coordinates unchanged. At each fixed p it is an
isometry in the continuous coordinates. Consequently

    Psi^(-1)_#(eta|_F_u)
       = sum_{p in P} H_(d-1)|_{D_p} = mu_u.              (7)

Every D_p is nonempty by (4), and the base is exactly P. Some of
these faces can have smaller dimension and zero measure. The assumed
positive sector mass ensures at least one has dimension d-1. The
finite disjoint trace therefore has Hausdorff dimension d-1 and its
intrinsic Hausdorff measure is exactly (7). In particular, for d=1
the reduced measure counts its singleton fibers.

There is no slope Jacobian in (7). If ambient facet area is separately
considered, the Jacobian of Psi is sqrt(1+|a|^2), and the coarea
Jacobian of base projection is its reciprocal. These factors are
not part of the discrete fiber measure. Pulling the restricted
physical martingale through the affine inverse proves (3), including
equal affine moments and without adding an incoming source term.

Suppose, in addition, the actual source has cap-allocation density

    dnu = (sum_j lambda_j alpha_j) deta.

Then its reduced density is exactly

    dnu_hat_u = (sum_j lambda_j alpha_j(Psi(z,t))) dmu_u.  (8)

For a closed ambient cap c_j.z+v_j.x>=beta_j, its restriction is

    (c_j+(v_j.u)a).z + (E^T v_j).t
        >= beta_j-(v_j.u)b.                             (9)

This includes all oblique, pure-base, whole-plane, and empty traces.
At positive-measure coincident cap boundaries, (8) keeps the original
allocation branch; it need not equal the closed indicator of (9).
If the boundary is mu_u-null, the indicator description is valid
almost everywhere. These are precisely the same distinctions as in
the corrected general supporting-facet law, with correction now zero.

## 4. Relation to globally Minkowski-affine families

If h_Kp(v)=a(v).p+b(v) for every unit direction v, then for any
convex combination z=sum_p theta_p p the Minkowski combination
sum_p theta_p K_p has support function a(v).z+b(v). It is therefore
independent of the representation of z. The section of C_0 at z is
exactly this body: arbitrary hull representations are such
Minkowski combinations, and every one yields that same body. Hence
the sampled hypothesis gives a genuinely Minkowski-affine family
throughout the canonical real-base hull.

There are only finitely many positive own-normal sectors for the
finite polytopal family. Applying the theorem to each yields a
finite decomposition of the full boundary martingale into exact
unweighted reduced volume transports. This is a sector-by-sector
conclusion, not a relation between the reduced facet volumes and
the original bulk cap budgets.

In this globally affine case with P spanning R^n, every nonvertical
facet of C_0 is one of the global support facets just described.
Indeed let such a facet have supporting functional c.z+v.x, with
v nonzero and u=v/|v|. Every point of the facet must maximize u.x
inside its own fiber; otherwise moving within that fiber would
increase the supporting functional. Thus the facet lies in F_u and
also in the base hyperplane

    (c+|v|a(u)).z = beta-|v|b(u).

If the displayed base coefficient were nonzero, this base hyperplane
and the F_u hyperplane would be independent (the latter has continuous
normal u). Their intersection has dimension at most n+d-2, contrary
to being a facet. Therefore c+|v|a(u)=0 and the facet is exactly F_u.
In particular it projects onto all of conv(P). Two distinct such
facets have different continuous unit normals; otherwise uniqueness
of affine interpolation on a spanning P would give the same plane.
Consequently almost every measured own-boundary point has a unique
nonvertical ambient facet owner in C_0. This also verifies the earlier
unique-ownership sufficient condition directly for this class. Facets
with zero sampled boundary measure do not affect that assertion.

If the affine support identity is instead assumed for every real
base of the original C, then the supporting plane already supports
C itself and no canonical replacement is needed. If it is assumed
only at integer bases, claiming that it supports the original C is
in general false. For example, in R times R take the hull of
{0,1} times [-1,1] together with (1/2,2). Its two positive-length
integer intervals both have upper support one,
while C contains a noninteger point strictly above x=1. Canonical
replacement restores the valid supporting plane without changing
any of the boundary measures or their physical transport law.

## 5. Exact nonconstant cap-law example and the limit of induction

Take n=1, C=[0,2] times [-1/2,1/2]^d, and integer bases 0,1,2.
Every continuous fiber has identical support function, so all the
above affine-support conclusions hold. On the full marked boundary
let the source density, by base, be

    f(0)=3/4,  f(1)=3/2,  f(2)=3/4.                    (10)

For every fixed boundary point x and its normal mark, send source
mass 3/4 at bases 0 and 2 to themselves. At base 1 send masses
1/4,1,1/4 to bases 0,1,2 respectively. The source row has total
mass 3/2 and physical mean (1,x). Each target base receives density
one. Thus this is a normal-preserving physical martingale on the
entire actual boundary, with everywhere positive source density.

It is even a positive weighted cap-indicator law:

    f = (3/4)(1_{z<=3/2}+1_{z>=1/2})

on all integer fibers. The two ambient cap boundaries miss every
integer fiber, so no allocation ambiguity is involved. With unit
fiber volumes their bulk budgets are both two, the total bulk mass
is three, and the coefficient-weighted budget sum is exactly three.
No cap-criticality or local depth minimality is asserted.

For u=e_1 the reduced body is

    D=[0,2] times [-1/2,1/2]^(d-1),

and its unweighted mixed volume has mass one at each base. The
inherited source density is still (10). Incoming mass is zero, but
the inherited law is not the unweighted target itself. For instance,
the convex test z^2 has source integral 9/2 and target integral 5.

When d>=2 the reduced source has positive (d-1)-dimensional volume
in the interior of every reduced fiber. The own-fiber boundary
measure of D, of dimension d-2, gives those interiors zero measure.
Therefore this inherited volume source cannot be reinterpreted as
an absolutely continuous reduced boundary stress. When d=1 the
reduced target is counting measure on singleton fibers, and a
recursive ordinary boundary measure is not present. This example
exhibits the distinction even with positive cap allocations and
zero incoming mass in every normal sector.

Thus the scoped conclusion is exact: affine sampled support eliminates
the incoming correction and gives unweighted lower-dimensional
volume transport. It does not supply lower-dimensional boundary
optimality conditions or identify restricted budgets with original
bulk budgets, and it does not close an OC induction.
